beats.concept: close-hauled: haul in the sheets and sail about 45 degrees off the wind
beats.gist: Leaving Lisboa with return cargo for the Ribatejo, the skipper sees the mark dead upwind and tells Zé they must haul in and work up in bordos, as sail-and-oar boats always did.

beats.concept: getting out of irons: bear away until the sails fill
beats.gist: The falua has pointed too high and stopped head to wind; the skipper gives a short instruction to bear away and fill the sails.

beats.concept: beating to windward: tacking between two close-hauled headings
beats.gist: Once moving again, the skipper explains to Zé that nobody sails straight into the wind: you hold about 45 degrees, then turn the bow through the wind and zigzag, and if in doubt you ease the sheets a little.

On a long steady bordo the skipper talks about the work: wine, cork and cereals going down to Lisboa, salt, manufactured goods, fertiliser and news coming back. He also mentions that sailors mix up boat names: a falua has two masts, while fragatas and varinos have one.
Looking back at the Lisboa quays, Zé remarks that this is where the river's goods and people arrive and leave, and the skipper adds that the river is the road for all that trade.

beats.concept: reaching an upwind mark by tacking
beats.gist: The mark is reached; the skipper tells Zé that ground won upwind is earned bordo by bordo, and that now the falua can carry on with her cargo upriver.

An optional card on how we know these boats: Manuel Fernandes's carpentry book gives construction details for a falua, and João de Souza's 1785 set of 20 engravings is the first credible picture record of Tagus boat types.

cast.name: Mestre Joaquim (fictional character)
cast.role: Invented skipper of a cargo falua, one of the embarcados who carried goods between Lisboa and the Ribatejo. Character in

cast.want: To work the falua upwind out of Lisboa without losing ground, so the return cargo reaches the river ports on time.

cast.name: Zé (fictional character)

evidence.text: Pinto Basto notes sailors confused boat names, calling fragatas and varinos 'faluas'; the falua has two masts, the others one, and they serve very different purposes. · who: A. J. Pinto Basto · place: Tejo · when: 1893
The fragata was a solid, open-mouthed, flat-sterned boat with one backward-leaning mast, a large gaff sail and one or two headsails, no oars, fixed rudder.
Fragatas varied in size, with a keeled hull and two cabins, one forward and one aft.
Fragata was a sturdy keeled boat with one raked mast, large gaff sail, one or two jibs, fixed rudder and no oars.
The term fragata was also commonly applied to similar-function boats such as faluas, medium-sized between bote and fragata. · place: Tejo

numbers: approximate angle to the wind when close-hauled: 45 degrees
evidence.text: Close-hauled: “bolina” (en) — Sailing as close to the wind as the rig permits, with sails tight; the only way to gain ground upwind, done by tacking.
Close-hauled: “Orça Fechada” (pt-BR) — Close-hauled: sailing as close to the wind line as possible, heading against it.
Tacking: “virar de bordo” (en) — Tacking: turning through the wind to change sides while going upwind, zigzagging between two close-hauled headings.
Tacking: “Cambar” (pt-BR) — Tacking: turning the bow through the wind line so the sails change sides.
Beating to windward: “Bordejar” (pt-BR) — Beating: sailing against the wind by making a series of tacks.

numbers: bow angle to wind line while beating: 45–50 degrees
turn per change of direction: 90–100 degrees
evidence.text: Beating to windward: “Bordejando” (pt-BR) — Tacking upwind: the only way to reach a destination lying toward the wind, by sailing a series of legs with the bow crossing the wind line.
Leg of a zigzag course: “bordo” (pt-BR) — A leg or tack of the zigzag course; changing tack is called giving a bordo.
Upwind trim rule: “Velejando contra o vento” (pt-BR) — Quick rule for sailing upwind: when in doubt, ease the sheets.
Upriver navigation (água acima): “água acima” (pt-PT) — Upriver. These boats were only permitted to sail in the calm river, not at sea beyond the bar.

evidence.location: [section: “O cais do vapor”, por Fernando Freire]
evidence.text: Upriver navigation (água acima): “ascenso e descenso” (pt-PT) — Travel upstream and downstream along the river, the way cargo and passengers moved between river ports.
